text: Lesson 17 built a real path between an Azure VNet and an AWS VPC — a VPN tunnel or a colocation meet-point, packets can now cross. That turns out to solve less than it feels like it should, because routing and naming are two different problems, and this lesson is entirely about the second one.

A service in Azure still can't ask 'where is orders-api dot internal' and get back a usable AWS address, because Azure's DNS has never heard of AWS's private zones, and AWS's resolver has never heard of Azure's. Without a shared resolution layer, the fallback is hardcoding IP addresses into config — and a cross-cloud private IP is exactly the address most likely to change, since it usually sits behind a load balancer, a NAT gateway, or an autoscaling group whose instances come and go. An IP that worked at deploy time is a production incident waiting for the next scale event.

The fix reuses the DNS Resolver model from hybrid on-premises connectivity, just pointed somewhere new. Azure's Private DNS Resolver has an inbound endpoint that accepts queries from outside Azure, and an outbound endpoint paired with forwarding rules that sends specific-domain queries out. Previously 'outside' meant on-premises; here it means AWS, reached over the Lesson 17 link. A forwarding rule for aws dot internal sends those queries across to AWS's resolver instead of failing to resolve locally.

AWS's Route 53 Resolver mirrors it exactly: an inbound endpoint accepts queries aimed at Route 53 private hosted zones, and an outbound endpoint plus a resolver rule forwards azure dot internal queries back across the link to Azure's inbound endpoint. Both directions need configuring, because a working query path one way says nothing about the other — bidirectional resolution isn't automatic just because the network path is.

That still leaves one organizational question: which cloud owns which names? The workable answer splits it cleanly by domain — Azure owns azure dot internal, AWS owns aws dot internal, and each Resolver just forwards into the other's territory. Nobody tries to run one unified zone split across two clouds' native DNS, because neither can be the sole source of truth for records the other cloud's control plane needs to write. With naming solved, the next real question is what actually talking across that link costs — that's Lesson 19.
